To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

flavonoids and dietary polyphenolic compounds are potent inhibitors of carcinogenesis, that they induce apoptosis in cancer cells, and that the molecular mechanisms of their actions are complex and involve many different molecular targets.

dietary flavonoids and other polyphenols can prevent chemical carcinogenesis in experimental animals, and that the molecular mechanisms of this chemoprevention involve the prevention of chemical carcinogenesis by inhibiting carcinogen metabolic activation and by preventing tumour cell growth and proliferation, and that the induction of tumours cell death (apotosis) is a major molecular mechanism for chemoprevention.

flavonoids and related polyphenolic compounds have a wide range of chemopreventative and therapeutic mechanisms of action that include: 1) inhibition of carcinogen metabolic activation; 2) inhibition of tumour cell proliferation through inactivation of pro-oxidant enzymes or downregulation or inhibition of signal transduction enzymes and 3) induction of tumour cells death by apoptosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the mechanisms of cancer chemoprevention and apoptosis induced by flavonoids and dietary polyphenolic compounds.
elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which dietary flavonoids or other polyphenols can prevent cancer.
the identification of dietary flavonoids and other polyphenols as chemopreventative agents against cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
flavonoids and other polyphenolic compounds have a potential role in cancer chemoprevention and/or cancer therapy by inducing apoptosis.

dietary flavonoids/polyphenols have a wide range of molecular mechanisms to prevent carcinogenesis and that the most promising mechanism for chemoprevention is the induction of apoptosis in tumour cells.
the molecular mechanisms for chemoprevention by polyphenols are still largely unclear and that more research is needed to clarify this issue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the administration of dietary flavonoids or phenolic antioxidants to animals can prevent the development of tumours in various organs and tissues.

the administration of polyphenols to experimental animals or human subjects has shown that these dietary compounds can prevent the initiation of tumours and/or the promotion of tumours, and that these compounds may also inhibit tumour progression and metastasis.
flavonoids and dietary polyphenols are promising candidates for cancer prevention and treatment, but the safety of these agents must be carefully monitored.
The main takeaway from our work is that
flavonoids and other polyphenols are potent inducers of apoptosis, and the mechanism for inducing apoptosis is through the mitochondria, as we have shown in our work.
the flavonoids/polyphenols that are safe for human consumption are also the ones that are effective for cancer chemoprevention.
